question.problem: A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ of $n$ people is drawn from a population. The population has people of two different weights, $78\,\text{kg}$ and $90\,\text{kg},$ distributed in the ratio $2:1.$ Determine the smallest sample size required so that the standard error of the mean is less than $0.1\,\text{kg}.$
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the people in the population have weights $78\,\text{kg}$ and $90\,\text{kg},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $2:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $2+1=3$ people only with the following weights:

$$
78\,\text{kg},\,78\,\text{kg},\,90\,\text{kg}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{3}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2\cdot 78+90) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(156+90) \\  & =\frac{246}{3} \\  & =82\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2\cdot {78}^{2}+{90}^{2})-{82}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(20\,268)-6\,724 \\  & =6\,756-6\,724 \\  & =32\,{\text{kg}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{32},$ and we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{32}{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.1\,\text{kg}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{32}{n}} & <0.1 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{32}}{0.1} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{32}{{0.1}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{3\,200} \\ n & >3\,200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest sample size is $n=3\,201.$
